Use AWS Lambda to process messages from the SQS queue with a concurrency limit of 100.
Use a fixed fleet of 5 Reserved Instances and 15 On-Demand instances for burst capacity.

explanation: Using an Auto Scaling group with Spot Instances that scales based on SQS queue depth is the most cost-effective approach. Spot Instances provide up to 90% savings, and scaling based on queue depth ensures enough capacity to process messages within the time constraint while not paying for idle resources during low-traffic periods. The 2-minute processing time is well suited for EC2 (Lambda has a 15-minute timeout but this workload needs sustained processing). Option A over-provisions with On-Demand instances. Option C could work but Lambda's per-invocation pricing may be more expensive for 2-minute executions at high volume. Option D commits to Reserved Instances when the workload is unpredictable.

stem: A company hosts a public-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The security team has identified that the application is vulnerable to SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. The team wants to implement a solution that blocks these attacks before they reach the application. Which AWS service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: AWS Shield Advanced to protect against SQL injection and XSS attacks.
AWS WAF with managed rule groups for SQL injection and XSS protection, deployed on an Application Load Balancer.
Amazon Inspector to scan the EC2 instances for SQL injection vulnerabilities.
Amazon GuardDuty to detect and block SQL injection and XSS attacks in real time.

explanation: AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) is specifically designed to protect web applications from common exploits like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. AWS Managed Rule groups provide pre-configured rules for these attack types. When deployed on an ALB, WAF inspects incoming HTTP requests and blocks malicious ones before they reach the application. Option A (Shield Advanced) protects against DDoS attacks, not application-layer attacks like SQLi and XSS. Option C (Inspector) scans for vulnerabilities in the infrastructure, not for active attacks. Option D (GuardDuty) detects threats but doesn't block web application attacks in real time.

stem: A company wants to build a data lake on Amazon S3. Multiple teams will upload data to the same S3 bucket simultaneously. The company needs to ensure that no data is lost or overwritten during concurrent uploads, even if two teams upload files with the same key at the same time. What should a solutions architect tell the teams about S3 consistency?

options.text: Amazon S3 provides eventual consistency for overwrite PUT requests. Teams must implement application-level locking to prevent data loss.
Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations. The last PUT to a key will win, so teams should use unique key prefixes to avoid conflicts.
Amazon S3 provides strong consistency only for new object PUTs, not for overwrite PUTs. Teams must use versioning to prevent data loss.
Amazon S3 does not support concurrent writes to the same key. Teams must use Amazon DynamoDB for write coordination.

explanation: Since December 2020, Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations, including overwrite PUTs and DELETEs. This means that after a PUT completes, any subsequent read will return the latest version. However, if two concurrent PUTs target the same key, the last one to complete will be the stored version (last-writer-wins). To prevent overwriting each other's data, teams should use unique key prefixes (e.g., team-name/date/filename). Option A is outdated; S3 no longer has eventual consistency. Option C incorrectly states that strong consistency is only for new objects. Option D is incorrect as S3 does support concurrent writes.

stem: A machine learning team needs to train deep learning models using large datasets stored in Amazon S3. The training jobs run on Amazon EC2 P4d instances and require high-throughput access to the training data. The dataset is 10 TB and is read multiple times during each training run. Which storage solution provides the best performance for this workload?

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket and mount it on the P4d instances.
Copy the training data from S3 to local NVMe instance store volumes on the P4d instances before training.
Use S3 directly with multi-threaded reads from the training application.
Create an Amazon EFS file system and copy the training data from S3 to EFS before training.

explanation: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system optimized for machine learning workloads. When linked to S3, it automatically loads data from S3 on first access and caches it, providing sub-millisecond latency for subsequent reads. This is ideal for iterative training where the dataset is read multiple times. FSx for Lustre can deliver hundreds of GB/s of throughput. Option B requires manual data copying and 10 TB may exceed instance store capacity. Option C has higher latency than a local file system, especially for random access patterns common in ML training. Option D uses EFS which has lower throughput than FSx for Lustre for this type of workload.

stem: A company has a hybrid architecture with an on-premises data center connected to AWS via AWS Direct Connect. The company wants to resolve DNS names for resources in both the on-premises data center and the AWS VPC. Currently, EC2 instances cannot resolve on-premises DNS names, and on-premises servers cannot resolve private AWS DNS names. Which solution resolves this bi-directional DNS issue?

options.text: Configure Amazon Route 53 Resolver with inbound endpoints for on-premises to AWS resolution and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for AWS to on-premises resolution.
Deploy a custom DNS server on an EC2 instance that forwards queries to both the on-premises DNS and the VPC DNS resolver.
Configure Route 53 public hosted zones for both the on-premises and AWS domains.
Enable DNS hostnames and DNS resolution in the VPC settings and update the DHCP option set with the on-premises DNS server IP.

explanation: Route 53 Resolver endpoints provide the managed solution for hybrid DNS resolution. Inbound endpoints allow on-premises DNS servers to forward queries for AWS-hosted domains to Route 53 Resolver, enabling on-premises servers to resolve private AWS DNS names. Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules allow the VPC DNS resolver to forward queries for on-premises domains to the on-premises DNS servers. This provides bi-directional resolution without managing custom DNS infrastructure. Option B requires managing a custom DNS server. Option C uses public hosted zones which don't provide private DNS resolution. Option D points VPC DNS to on-premises servers but breaks AWS-native DNS resolution.

stem: A company has multiple AWS Lambda functions that process events from Amazon SQS queues. Each Lambda function runs for an average of 100 milliseconds and uses 256 MB of memory. The company processes 100 million events per month. A developer proposes increasing the memory to 512 MB, which would reduce the execution time to 50 milliseconds. Should the company implement this change from a cost perspective?

options.text: No, because doubling the memory will double the cost, even though execution time is halved.
Yes, because the total GB-seconds of compute will remain the same while providing faster processing.
No, because Lambda pricing is based only on the number of invocations, not on memory or execution time.
Yes, because reducing execution time always reduces Lambda costs regardless of memory allocation.

explanation: Lambda pricing is based on GB-seconds (memory allocated multiplied by execution time). With 256 MB and 100 ms: 0.25 GB x 0.1s = 0.025 GB-seconds per invocation. With 512 MB and 50 ms: 0.5 GB x 0.05s = 0.025 GB-seconds per invocation. The total GB-seconds are the same, so the cost is approximately the same, but the function runs twice as fast, providing better performance at no additional cost. Option A is incorrect because it doesn't account for the reduced execution time. Option C is wrong because Lambda charges for both invocations and compute duration (GB-seconds). Option D is an over-generalization; reducing execution time doesn't always offset the cost of higher memory.

stem: A company runs a mission-critical application that uses an Amazon RDS Oracle database. The database team needs to perform a major version upgrade with minimal downtime. The current database is 2 TB in size. Which approach minimizes downtime during the upgrade?

options.text: Take a snapshot of the current database, restore it with the new version, test it, and then switch the application connection string during a maintenance window.
Create a read replica with the new Oracle version, let it sync, then promote it to a standalone instance and switch the application to the new instance.
Use the RDS Blue/Green Deployments feature to create a green environment with the new version, test it, and then perform a switchover.
Perform an in-place major version upgrade during a maintenance window and accept the downtime.

explanation: RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a staging environment (green) that mirrors the production environment (blue) with logical replication to keep data in sync. The green environment can be upgraded to the new major version and thoroughly tested while the blue environment continues serving traffic. When ready, the switchover happens in about a minute with minimal downtime. Option A requires significant downtime to restore a 2 TB snapshot. Option B is not supported for major Oracle version upgrades via read replicas. Option D results in extended downtime, especially for a 2 TB database major version upgrade.

stem: A news organization needs to deliver live video streams to millions of concurrent viewers worldwide during major events. The video streams must have low latency (under 10 seconds) and adapt to varying network conditions. Which architecture should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Elemental MediaLive to encode live video, AWS Elemental MediaPackage to package the stream with adaptive bitrate, and Amazon CloudFront to distribute the content globally.
Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to ingest live video and serve it directly to viewers through a custom web application.
Use Amazon EC2 instances running FFmpeg for encoding and serve the streams through an Application Load Balancer.
Upload live video segments to Amazon S3 and use S3 Transfer Acceleration to serve them globally.

explanation: AWS Elemental MediaLive handles live video encoding, MediaPackage provides adaptive bitrate packaging (HLS, DASH) that adjusts quality based on viewer network conditions, and CloudFront distributes content from edge locations worldwide for low latency. This is the recommended AWS architecture for large-scale live streaming. Option B is designed for video analytics and playback, not live broadcasting to millions of viewers. Option C requires managing EC2 instances and cannot scale to millions of concurrent viewers. Option D is not designed for live streaming and would introduce significant latency.

stem: A company is implementing a defense-in-depth strategy for its VPC. The company wants to control traffic at multiple layers. Which TWO combinations of AWS services provide network security at different layers? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Security groups for instance-level stateful traffic filtering
Network ACLs for subnet-level stateless traffic filtering
AWS Shield for instance-level stateful traffic filtering
Amazon Inspector for subnet-level traffic filtering
AWS Config for real-time network traffic blocking

explanation: Security groups operate at the instance (ENI) level and are stateful, meaning return traffic is automatically allowed regardless of outbound rules. Network ACLs operate at the subnet level and are stateless, meaning both inbound and outbound rules must explicitly allow traffic. Together they provide defense-in-depth with traffic filtering at two different levels. Option C is incorrect because Shield protects against DDoS attacks, not instance-level traffic filtering. Option D is incorrect because Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service, not a traffic filtering tool. Option E is incorrect because Config monitors configuration compliance, not network traffic.

stem: A company has a data warehouse running on Amazon Redshift with 10 dc2.large nodes. The cluster is used heavily for complex queries during business hours but has very low utilization during nights and weekends. The company wants to reduce costs without affecting daytime performance. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift Serverless instead of a provisioned cluster, allowing capacity to scale automatically based on workload demands.
Schedule snapshots and delete the cluster each night, then restore it each morning before business hours.
Reduce the number of nodes to 5 and enable concurrency scaling for peak demand.
Migrate from Redshift to Amazon Athena for all data warehouse queries.

explanation: Amazon Redshift Serverless automatically scales compute capacity based on workload demands and you only pay for the compute you use. During low-utilization periods (nights and weekends), costs are minimal since there is little to no query activity. During business hours, it scales up to handle complex queries. This eliminates the cost of idle provisioned nodes. Option B involves significant operational overhead and risk with daily cluster deletion and restoration. Option C reduces capacity permanently which may impact daytime performance. Option D would require significant query rewrites and may not provide the same performance for complex data warehouse queries.

stem: A company is designing an architecture for a globally distributed application. Users in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific need low-latency access to the same dataset. The data is updated frequently and all users must see consistent data within 1 second of an update. Which database solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB global tables with multi-Region replication.
Amazon Aurora Global Database with read replicas in each Region.
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ with cross-Region read replicas.
Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore with Redis clusters in each Region.

explanation: DynamoDB global tables provide fully replicated, multi-Region, multi-active database tables. Data written in any Region is replicated to all other Regions typically within 1 second, meeting the consistency requirement. All Regions can accept both reads and writes, providing low-latency access for users worldwide. Option B provides cross-Region read replicas but writes must go to the primary Region, adding latency for non-primary Region users. Option C has higher replication lag and writes are limited to the primary Region. Option D provides caching but is not suitable as a primary data store for frequently updated data requiring cross-Region consistency.

stem: A company is building a mobile application that allows users to upload photos. The application uses Amazon Cognito for authentication. The company wants authenticated users to upload photos directly to an Amazon S3 bucket without routing traffic through the application servers. How should a solutions architect implement this?

options.text: Create an IAM user for the mobile app with permissions to write to S3, and embed the access keys in the mobile application.
Configure Amazon Cognito identity pools to provide temporary AWS credentials with an IAM role that allows S3 PutObject access to a user-specific prefix.
Generate pre-signed S3 URLs on the server side for each upload request and return them to the mobile app.
Create an S3 bucket policy that allows public write access and validate uploads using an S3 event-triggered Lambda function.

explanation: Amazon Cognito identity pools (federated identities) can provide temporary, scoped AWS credentials to authenticated users. By configuring an IAM role with fine-grained S3 permissions (e.g., allowing PutObject to s3://bucket/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*), each user gets temporary credentials that only allow uploads to their own prefix. This is secure, scalable, and serverless. Option A embeds long-term credentials in the app, which is a security anti-pattern. Option C works but requires server-side infrastructure to generate URLs, adding latency and operational overhead. Option D allows public write access which is a major security risk.

stem: A retail company runs an order management system on Amazon EC2 instances. The system writes orders to an Amazon RDS MySQL database. During a recent database failover, some orders were lost because the application did not handle the database connection errors correctly. The company wants to prevent order loss during future failover events without modifying the application code. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Place an Amazon SQS queue between the application and the database. Write orders to SQS first, then use a separate consumer to write to RDS.
Enable RDS Proxy between the application and the database to handle connection management and failover automatically.
Configure the RDS instance with a larger instance class to reduce failover time.
Add multiple read replicas and configure the application to write to a read replica if the primary is unavailable.

explanation: Placing an SQS queue between the application and database decouples the write operation. Orders are first written to the durable SQS queue (which guarantees message delivery), then a separate consumer process writes them to RDS. During a database failover, orders remain safely in the queue until the database becomes available again, preventing any data loss. This approach doesn't require application code changes for the order submission path. Option B helps with connection management but doesn't prevent data loss if the database is temporarily unavailable. Option C doesn't prevent order loss during failover. Option D is incorrect because read replicas cannot accept write operations.

stem: A company runs a content management system (CMS) that serves web pages with a mix of static and dynamic content. The static content (images, CSS, JavaScript) changes infrequently, while the dynamic content (user-specific data) changes with every request. The company wants to improve page load times globally. Which approach should a solutions architect take?

options.text: Serve all content through Amazon CloudFront with a single cache behavior and a short TTL of 10 seconds.
Configure Amazon CloudFront with multiple cache behaviors: long TTL for static content and cache disabled (forwarding all headers) for dynamic content paths.
Serve static content from Amazon S3 and dynamic content from EC2 without using a CDN.
Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache both static and dynamic content at the application layer.

explanation: CloudFront cache behaviors allow different caching policies for different URL patterns. Static content (images, CSS, JS) can be cached with long TTLs (e.g., 24 hours) at edge locations for fast delivery, while dynamic content paths can be configured to forward all requests to the origin with no caching or short TTLs. This maximizes cache hit ratios for static content while ensuring dynamic content is always fresh. Option A uses a single TTL which either over-caches dynamic content or under-caches static content. Option C loses the global performance benefits of a CDN for static content. Option D caches at the application layer, not at the edge, and doesn't help with global delivery.

stem: A company runs a web application on three m5.xlarge Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances 24/7. AWS Compute Optimizer shows that the average CPU utilization is 10% with occasional spikes to 40%. The application is containerized using Docker. Which migration strategy would reduce costs the MOST?

options.text: Right-size the instances to m5.large based on the utilization data.
Migrate the containers to AWS Fargate with appropriate CPU and memory limits, using Fargate Spot for non-critical tasks.
Purchase 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the m5.xlarge instances.
Migrate to AWS Lambda and convert the application to a serverless architecture.

explanation: Migrating to AWS Fargate eliminates the need to manage EC2 instances and you only pay for the vCPU and memory that your containers actually use. With only 10% average CPU utilization, the current EC2 instances are significantly over-provisioned. Fargate allows precise resource allocation per container, and Fargate Spot provides additional savings for non-critical tasks. Since the application is already containerized, migration is straightforward. Option A reduces costs by ~50% but still wastes capacity at 10% utilization on smaller instances. Option C locks in costs for over-provisioned instances. Option D requires significant application refactoring from a web application to serverless functions.

stem: A company needs to grant temporary access to a third-party auditing firm to review resources in the company's AWS account. The audit will take 2 weeks. The company wants to follow the principle of least privilege and ensure access is automatically revoked after the audit period. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create IAM users for each auditor with ReadOnly access and delete the users after 2 weeks.
Create an IAM role with ReadOnly access and a trust policy allowing the auditing firm's AWS account to assume it. Set a maximum session duration and use a condition with an expiration date.
Share the AWS account root credentials with the auditing firm and change the password after 2 weeks.
Create a VPN connection to the auditing firm's network and whitelist their IP addresses in security groups.

explanation: Creating an IAM role with cross-account access follows AWS best practices for granting temporary third-party access. The trust policy can specify the auditor's AWS account as the trusted principal, and a condition with aws:CurrentTime can automatically expire access after 2 weeks. The role has ReadOnly permissions following least privilege. No long-term credentials are shared. Option A creates IAM users with long-term credentials and requires manual deletion. Option C sharing root credentials is a critical security anti-pattern. Option D doesn't grant AWS resource access and isn't related to auditing AWS resources.

stem: A company processes financial transactions through a microservices architecture. When a new order is placed, it must trigger updates in the inventory service, billing service, and notification service. If any service is temporarily unavailable, the message must not be lost and should be delivered when the service recovers. Which messaging pattern should a solutions architect use?

options.text: Use Amazon SNS with SQS subscriptions for each service (fan-out pattern). Each service has its own SQS queue subscribed to the SNS topic.
Use direct API calls from the order service to each downstream service with retry logic.
Use a single Amazon SQS queue that all three services poll from.
Use Amazon EventBridge with a single target Lambda function that calls all three services sequentially.

explanation: The SNS-SQS fan-out pattern is ideal for this scenario. When an order is placed, a message is published to an SNS topic. Each downstream service (inventory, billing, notification) has its own SQS queue subscribed to the topic. SNS delivers a copy of the message to each queue. If a service is temporarily unavailable, its messages remain in its SQS queue until the service recovers and processes them. This ensures no message is lost and each service processes independently. Option B creates tight coupling and doesn't guarantee delivery if services are down. Option C would cause only one service to receive each message. Option D has a single point of failure and sequential processing.

stem: A company needs to run a relational database workload that requires 64,000 IOPS of consistent performance. The database is 500 GB in size. Which Amazon EBS volume type should a solutions architect choose?

options.text: General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume with provisioned IOPS set to 64,000.
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with 64,000 IOPS provisioned.
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume with a large size for higher baseline throughput.
General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume with default settings and RAID 0 across 4 volumes.

explanation: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes support up to 64,000 IOPS per volume and provide consistent, predictable performance. io2 volumes are designed for I/O-intensive workloads that require sustained IOPS performance, making them ideal for demanding database workloads. Option A is incorrect because gp3 volumes support a maximum of 16,000 IOPS, which is insufficient. Option C uses HDD volumes which measure performance in throughput (MB/s), not IOPS, and provide much lower IOPS. Option D with RAID 0 across gp3 volumes adds complexity and has potential reliability concerns while still being limited by per-volume IOPS caps.

stem: A company wants to reduce its AWS data transfer costs. The company has applications in us-east-1 that communicate with services in eu-west-1. The monthly cross-Region data transfer is 10 TB. Which TWO strategies can reduce data transfer costs? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Compress data before transferring it between Regions to reduce the volume of data transferred.
Use VPC peering between the Regions instead of transferring data over the public internet.
Replicate the necessary data and services to the same Region to eliminate cross-Region transfers.
Use AWS Direct Connect between the two Regions to avoid data transfer charges.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for all cross-Region data transfers.

explanation: Compressing data before cross-Region transfer directly reduces the volume of data transferred and therefore the cost. If 10 TB compresses to 3 TB, that is a 70% reduction in transfer costs. Replicating data and services to the same Region eliminates cross-Region transfer entirely, which is the most effective cost reduction. Option B uses VPC peering but cross-Region VPC peering still incurs the same data transfer charges as standard cross-Region transfer. Option D does not connect two AWS Regions and wouldn't eliminate inter-Region transfer fees. Option E increases transfer speed but does not reduce the data transfer charges.

stem: A company stores sensitive customer data in Amazon S3. Compliance requires that the company track all API calls made to the S3 bucket, including which IAM principal accessed which objects and when. This data must be retained for 5 years. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 server access logging and store the logs in a separate S3 bucket with a 5-year retention Lifecycle policy.
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for S3 and configure the trail to deliver logs to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode for 5 years.
Enable Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the S3 bucket and set the log group retention to 5 years.
Enable S3 Inventory reports and store them in a separate bucket for auditing purposes.

explanation: AWS CloudTrail data events for S3 capture detailed API activity including the IAM principal, the action performed, the object accessed, and the timestamp. Delivering logs to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode ensures the logs cannot be deleted or modified for 5 years, meeting the compliance retention requirement. Option A provides access logs but with less detail about IAM principals and API calls compared to CloudTrail. Option C is not a native S3 logging mechanism. Option D provides inventory reports about what's stored in S3, not API access tracking.

stem: A company has an application that uses Amazon DynamoDB. The application occasionally experiences spikes in read traffic that exceed the provisioned capacity, causing throttling errors. The application can tolerate eventually consistent reads. Which solution addresses the throttling with the LEAST cost?

options.text: Switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode.
Increase the provisioned read capacity units to handle peak traffic.
Use eventually consistent reads instead of strongly consistent reads to double the effective read throughput.
Add DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache frequently read items.

explanation: Eventually consistent reads consume half the read capacity units compared to strongly consistent reads. Since the application can tolerate eventually consistent reads, switching from strongly consistent to eventually consistent reads effectively doubles the read throughput without any additional cost. This is the least expensive solution as it requires no infrastructure changes or additional services. Option A may increase costs during spikes since on-demand pricing is higher per-unit. Option B increases the provisioned capacity and therefore the base cost. Option D adds DAX which introduces additional infrastructure costs.

stem: A company runs a web application that receives 10,000 requests per second. Each request requires a database lookup that takes 50 milliseconds. The application uses Amazon RDS PostgreSQL, and the database CPU is at 90% utilization. Most queries are read operations fetching user profile data. Which solution should a solutions architect implement to reduce the database load?

options.text: Vertically scale the RDS instance to a larger instance type with more CPU.
Add Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database and cache user profile data with a TTL appropriate for the data freshness requirements.
Convert from RDS PostgreSQL to Amazon DynamoDB for faster read performance.
Enable Multi-AZ deployment on the RDS instance to distribute read queries.

explanation: ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond read latency and can handle millions of requests per second. By caching user profile data (which is read-heavy), the vast majority of read requests will be served from the cache instead of hitting the database, dramatically reducing the database CPU from 90% to a much lower level. Option A only provides temporary relief as traffic grows and is more expensive. Option C requires significant application refactoring to change from relational to NoSQL. Option D is incorrect because Multi-AZ standby instances do not serve read traffic; they are only for failover.

stem: A company uses AWS Lambda functions triggered by Amazon API Gateway. The Lambda functions query Amazon DynamoDB and return results. The company notices that 80% of API requests return the same data that changes only once per hour. The company wants to reduce both Lambda invocation costs and DynamoDB read costs. Which solution achieves this?

options.text: Enable API Gateway caching with a TTL of 3600 seconds for the frequently requested endpoints.
Increase the DynamoDB provisioned read capacity to reduce throttling.
Use Lambda provisioned concurrency to keep functions warm and reduce cold start latency.
Implement a DAX cluster to cache DynamoDB reads.

explanation: API Gateway caching serves repeated requests directly from the cache without invoking the Lambda function at all. With a TTL of 3600 seconds (1 hour), matching the data refresh rate, 80% of requests would be served from cache. This eliminates both Lambda invocation costs (no function execution) and DynamoDB read costs (no database queries) for cached responses. Option B doesn't reduce costs; it increases them. Option C reduces cold start latency but doesn't reduce the number of invocations. Option D reduces DynamoDB latency but still triggers Lambda for every request, not reducing Lambda costs.

stem: A company has deployed an application in a private subnet that needs to access Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB. The company's security policy requires that no traffic from the application should traverse the public internet. The VPC does not have a NAT gateway or internet gateway. Which configuration enables access to both S3 and DynamoDB?

options.text: Create VPC gateway endpoints for both S3 and DynamoDB, and add routes to the private subnet route table.
Create VPC interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for both S3 and DynamoDB.
Add a NAT gateway in a public subnet to allow the private subnet to access AWS services.
Configure the application to use the AWS SDK with the --endpoint-url flag pointing to the service's regional endpoint.

explanation: Both S3 and DynamoDB support VPC gateway endpoints. Gateway endpoints are free, don't require a NAT gateway or internet gateway, and route traffic through the AWS private network. Adding routes to the subnet route table directs S3 and DynamoDB traffic through the endpoints instead of the internet. This satisfies the security requirement of no public internet traffic. Option B is technically possible for S3 (which supports both gateway and interface endpoints) but DynamoDB only supports gateway endpoints, not interface endpoints. Option C introduces a NAT gateway which routes traffic through an internet gateway. Option D doesn't change the network path; the SDK still needs a network route to reach the endpoints.

stem: A company is designing a disaster recovery strategy for an application that uses Amazon EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS database. The application requires an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 1 hour. Which TWO components should be included in the disaster recovery plan? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Create automated RDS snapshots every hour and copy them to the DR Region.
Deploy a fully running duplicate of the application in the DR Region (hot standby).
Maintain AMIs of the EC2 instances in the DR Region and use AWS CloudFormation to quickly launch the infrastructure during a disaster.
Perform manual database backups weekly and store them on tape in an offsite location.
Use Amazon S3 cross-Region replication with a 24-hour replication schedule.

explanation: Hourly RDS snapshots copied to the DR Region ensure the RPO of 1 hour is met, as the maximum data loss would be 1 hour of transactions. Maintaining AMIs and CloudFormation templates in the DR Region enables a pilot light or warm standby approach where the infrastructure can be launched within the 4-hour RTO. This is a cost-effective approach that meets both requirements. Option B (hot standby) would work but is unnecessarily expensive for a 4-hour RTO. Option D weekly manual backups result in an RPO of up to 1 week, far exceeding the 1-hour requirement. Option E with 24-hour replication exceeds the 1-hour RPO requirement.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy monolithic application to a microservices architecture on AWS. The application needs a message broker that supports multiple messaging protocols including AMQP, MQTT, and STOMP. The company wants to minimize the effort of migrating the messaging layer. Which AWS service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Amazon SQS with Amazon SNS for pub/sub messaging.
Amazon MQ with an ActiveMQ broker.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time message processing.
Amazon EventBridge for event-driven messaging between microservices.

explanation: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service that supports Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. ActiveMQ supports multiple messaging protocols including AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire, and WebSocket. This makes it ideal for migrating legacy applications that use industry-standard messaging protocols with minimal code changes. Option A only supports the AWS-native SQS/SNS protocols, requiring application changes. Option C is designed for streaming data, not traditional message queuing with specific protocol requirements. Option D is an event bus service that doesn't support standard messaging protocols like AMQP or MQTT.

stem: A company has a DynamoDB table with 100 GB of data using provisioned capacity mode. The table receives consistent traffic with predictable read and write patterns during the day but almost zero traffic at night. The company is paying for provisioned capacity 24/7 even though the table is idle for 12 hours daily. Which solution optimizes costs while maintaining performance during peak hours?

options.text: Switch to on-demand capacity mode for the DynamoDB table.
Use DynamoDB Auto Scaling with appropriate minimum and maximum capacity settings and a target utilization of 70%.
Manually adjust the provisioned capacity using a scheduled AWS Lambda function.
Migrate the data to Amazon Aurora Serverless for automatic scaling.

explanation: DynamoDB Auto Scaling automatically adjusts provisioned capacity based on actual traffic patterns. By setting appropriate minimum and maximum values, the table scales up during the day for peak traffic and scales down during the night when traffic is near zero, significantly reducing costs. A target utilization of 70% provides headroom for traffic variations. Option A (on-demand) may be more expensive than provisioned with Auto Scaling for predictable traffic patterns, as on-demand per-unit pricing is higher. Option C achieves similar results but with more operational overhead than Auto Scaling. Option D requires migrating to a completely different database technology.

stem: A company is running an application that processes credit card payments. The application must comply with PCI DSS requirements. The company wants to ensure that the EC2 instances running the payment processing application are hardened and continuously assessed for vulnerabilities. Which AWS service should a solutions architect recommend for automated vulnerability assessment?

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor to check for security best practices.
Amazon Inspector to automatically assess EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.
AWS Config to monitor configuration changes on EC2 instances.
Amazon GuardDuty to detect security threats on EC2 instances.

explanation: Amazon Inspector is an automated vulnerability management service that continually scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure. It provides detailed findings with severity ratings and remediation guidance, which is essential for PCI DSS compliance. Inspector automatically discovers and begins assessing instances in the account. Option A provides broad best-practice recommendations but not detailed vulnerability assessments of specific instances. Option C monitors configuration compliance but doesn't scan for software vulnerabilities. Option D detects active threats and anomalous behavior but doesn't assess software vulnerabilities.

stem: A company runs a stateless web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group uses a target tracking scaling policy based on CPU utilization with a target of 60%. During a sudden traffic spike, new instances take 5 minutes to start and become healthy, causing degraded performance. How should a solutions architect reduce the time to handle traffic spikes?

options.text: Change the scaling policy to a step scaling policy with aggressive scale-out thresholds.
Configure a warm pool for the Auto Scaling group with pre-initialized instances in a stopped state.
Increase the maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group.
Reduce the target CPU utilization to 30% to trigger scaling earlier.

explanation: A warm pool maintains pre-initialized EC2 instances in a stopped state. When a scale-out event occurs, instances from the warm pool can be started much faster (typically under a minute) compared to launching new instances from scratch (which requires instance launch, OS boot, application deployment, and health check). This significantly reduces the time to respond to traffic spikes. Option A changes the scaling trigger but doesn't reduce instance launch time. Option C allows more instances but doesn't speed up their launch. Option D triggers scaling earlier but instances still take 5 minutes to become healthy.

stem: A company has a data pipeline that ingests 1 million small JSON records per second from IoT devices. Each record is approximately 1 KB. The data must be available for real-time analytics and also stored in a data lake for batch processing. Which ingestion architecture handles this throughput?

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with multiple shards for real-time analytics, and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver data to Amazon S3 for the data lake.
Use Amazon SQS to queue records and Lambda to process and store them in S3.
Write records directly to Amazon S3 using multipart uploads from each IoT device.
Use Amazon API Gateway to receive records and forward them to AWS Step Functions for processing.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams can handle millions of records per second across multiple shards, supporting real-time analytics use cases. Each shard handles 1,000 records/second or 1 MB/second for writes. For 1 million records/second, approximately 1,000 shards are needed. Kinesis Data Firehose can simultaneously deliver the same data to S3 for the data lake, creating a dual-purpose architecture. Option B cannot handle 1 million messages per second reliably and Lambda has concurrency limits. Option C creates millions of individual S3 PutObject requests per second which is impractical. Option D has API Gateway limits (10,000 requests/second by default) and Step Functions is not designed for high-throughput stream processing.

stem: A company wants to enable single sign-on (SSO) for its employees to access multiple AWS accounts and third-party SaaS applications. The company uses Microsoft Active Directory on-premises for identity management. Which solution provides SSO with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO) with AD Connector to connect to the on-premises Active Directory.
Set up SAML 2.0 federation individually for each AWS account and SaaS application.
Replicate Active Directory users as IAM users in each AWS account.
Deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and establish a one-way trust with the on-premises Active Directory.

explanation: AWS IAM Identity Center provides a centralized SSO portal for accessing multiple AWS accounts and SaaS applications. AD Connector creates a lightweight proxy that redirects authentication requests to the on-premises Active Directory without requiring directory synchronization. This provides the least operational overhead as IAM Identity Center manages permission sets and assignments centrally. Option B requires setting up SAML federation separately for each application, which is operationally expensive. Option C requires creating and managing individual IAM users, which doesn't scale and doesn't provide true SSO. Option D deploys a full Active Directory which has higher cost and operational overhead than AD Connector.

stem: A company uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy its infrastructure. During a recent deployment, a CloudFormation stack update failed, leaving some resources in an inconsistent state. The company wants to ensure that future failed updates automatically roll back to the previous working state. Which CloudFormation feature should a solutions architect configure?

options.text: Enable stack termination protection to prevent accidental deletion.
Configure automatic rollback on failure for stack updates, which is enabled by default.
Use CloudFormation drift detection to identify configuration changes.
Create a CloudFormation change set before every update and manually review it.

explanation: CloudFormation automatic rollback on failure is enabled by default for stack updates. When a stack update fails, CloudFormation automatically rolls back all changes to the previous known good state. If this was somehow disabled using --disable-rollback for debugging, re-enabling it ensures consistency. The solution architect should verify this setting is active and not overridden. Option A prevents stack deletion but doesn't affect update failure behavior. Option C detects drift from the template but doesn't handle update failures. Option D provides change review but doesn't address automatic recovery from failures.

stem: A company needs to analyze terabytes of structured data stored in Amazon S3 using standard SQL queries. The data is in Parquet format and partitioned by date. Queries typically scan data from the last 7 days. The company wants to minimize costs and does not need sub-second query response times. Which service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Load the data into Amazon Redshift and run SQL queries against the cluster.
Use Amazon Athena to run SQL queries directly on the data in S3, leveraging partition pruning for the date-based partitions.
Set up an Amazon EMR cluster with Hive to query the data in S3.
Import the data into Amazon RDS and create indexes on the date column for efficient queries.

explanation: Amazon Athena is serverless and charges only for the data scanned by each query. Since the data is in Parquet (columnar format) and partitioned by date, Athena can leverage partition pruning to scan only the last 7 days of data, minimizing costs. There is no infrastructure to manage, and the pay-per-query model is ideal for intermittent analysis. Option A requires provisioning and paying for a Redshift cluster. Option C requires managing an EMR cluster. Option D is impractical for terabytes of data and RDS is not designed for analytical workloads.

stem: A company has multiple development teams that each manage their own AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. The company wants to share common resources like VPC subnets, Transit Gateway, and AWS License Manager configurations across accounts without duplicating them. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use?

options.text: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) to share resources across accounts within the organization.
AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy identical resources in each account.
VPC peering between all accounts to share network resources.
AWS Service Catalog to provision pre-approved resources in each account.

explanation: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) enables sharing AWS resources across accounts within an organization. RAM supports sharing VPC subnets, Transit Gateway, License Manager configurations, and many other resource types. This avoids duplicating resources in each account, reducing costs and operational overhead. Option B deploys separate copies of resources in each account, which is duplication. Option C creates peer connections but doesn't share resources like subnets or License Manager. Option D provisions resources in each account from a catalog but doesn't share them.

stem: A company's security team wants to be alerted immediately when any root user activity occurs in any of their AWS accounts managed by AWS Organizations. Which solution provides real-time alerting for root user API activity?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each account that matches AWS Console Sign-In events for the root user and targets an SNS topic.
Configure an organization-wide CloudTrail trail and create an Amazon EventBridge rule in the management account that matches root user API calls, targeting an SNS topic for alerts.
Enable AWS Config rules in each account to detect root user access and send notifications.
Use Amazon GuardDuty to detect root user activity and configure SNS notifications.

explanation: An organization-wide CloudTrail trail captures API activity from all accounts in the organization. An EventBridge rule in the management account can match CloudTrail events where the userIdentity type is 'Root', triggering an SNS notification for real-time alerting. This centralized approach covers all accounts without needing individual configuration in each account. Option A only captures console sign-in events, not all API activity, and requires configuration in every account. Option C doesn't directly detect root user API activity in real time. Option D detects specific threat patterns but may not alert on all root user activities.

stem: A SaaS company hosts a multi-tenant application where each tenant's data must be isolated. The application uses Amazon DynamoDB for data storage. During peak hours, some tenants with heavy usage cause throttling that affects other tenants. How should a solutions architect prevent a single tenant from impacting others?

options.text: Create a separate DynamoDB table for each tenant.
Use a single DynamoDB table with tenant ID as the partition key and implement request throttling at the application layer using token bucket algorithms per tenant.
Increase the DynamoDB provisioned capacity to handle the heaviest tenant's peak usage.
Move all tenants to DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode.

explanation: Using tenant ID as the partition key ensures each tenant's data is distributed across different partitions, providing natural isolation in DynamoDB. Implementing application-layer throttling with token bucket algorithms limits each tenant's request rate, preventing any single tenant from consuming disproportionate capacity and causing hot partitions. This is the recommended multi-tenant design pattern. Option A creates operational overhead with thousands of tables and increases costs. Option C wastes capacity for most tenants. Option D removes provisioned capacity limits but hot partition issues can still cause throttling for specific partition keys.

stem: A company needs to build a real-time recommendation engine for its e-commerce platform. The engine must process user clickstream data and provide personalized product recommendations within 100 milliseconds. Which TWO services should a solutions architect include in the architecture? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Amazon Personalize for generating real-time personalized recommendations.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for ingesting real-time clickstream data.
Amazon Redshift for storing and querying user behavior patterns.
AWS Glue for real-time data transformation of clickstream events.
Amazon SageMaker batch transform for generating daily recommendation batches.

explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can ingest real-time clickstream data with millisecond latency, enabling the system to capture user behavior as it happens. Amazon Personalize provides real-time recommendation APIs that can return personalized product recommendations within milliseconds, meeting the 100ms requirement. Together, they enable real-time event ingestion and instant recommendation serving. Option C is a data warehouse not suited for real-time processing. Option D is a batch ETL service, not real-time. Option E generates recommendations in batch mode, not real-time.

stem: A company runs an internal tool on a single t3.medium Amazon EC2 instance. The tool is used by 10 employees during business hours. The company wants to move to a serverless architecture to eliminate the need for instance management. The tool is a simple CRUD application with a web frontend. Which architecture is MOST cost-effective for this low-traffic application?

options.text: Host the frontend on Amazon S3 with CloudFront. Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda for the backend and Amazon DynamoDB for the database.
Deploy the application on Amazon ECS Fargate with an Application Load Balancer.
Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk with a single instance environment.
Deploy the application on Amazon EKS with Fargate pods.

explanation: For a low-traffic internal tool used by 10 employees, a fully serverless architecture with S3 (static hosting), API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB is the most cost-effective. These services have generous free tiers and pay-per-use pricing. With minimal traffic, the costs would be near zero. S3 hosting is pennies per month, API Gateway and Lambda would stay within free tier limits, and DynamoDB on-demand pricing for a few users would be minimal. Option B requires paying for Fargate tasks and an ALB (minimum ~$16/month). Option C still runs an EC2 instance. Option D is the most expensive option with EKS cluster costs (~$73/month) plus Fargate costs.

stem: A company operates in a regulated industry and must ensure that all Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted. The company has hundreds of EC2 instances across multiple accounts and wants to prevent the launch of instances with unencrypted EBS volumes. Which approach provides enforcement at scale?

options.text: Enable EBS encryption by default in each account and Region where instances are launched.
Use AWS Config rules to detect unencrypted EBS volumes and send notifications.
Create an IAM policy that denies ec2:CreateVolume when the encrypted parameter is false.
Use a Lambda function to check newly created volumes and encrypt them if they are unencrypted.

explanation: Enabling EBS encryption by default ensures that all newly created EBS volumes and snapshots are automatically encrypted without requiring any additional configuration on each instance launch. This is the simplest and most effective enforcement mechanism. Once enabled, all new volumes in that account and Region are encrypted automatically, even if the user doesn't specify encryption. Option B is detective, not preventive - it finds unencrypted volumes after they're created. Option C adds complexity and must be maintained across all accounts. Option D is reactive rather than preventive and adds operational overhead.

stem: A company runs a critical API service that must maintain 99.99% availability. The API is currently deployed in a single AWS Region using an Application Load Balancer, EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, and Amazon Aurora. The company wants to achieve the availability target. Which architecture enhancement is MOST important?

options.text: Deploy the API in a second Region with identical infrastructure, use Aurora Global Database, and configure Route 53 with health checks and failover routing.
Add more Availability Zones to the current Region's deployment.
Enable Aurora Multi-AZ and increase the number of EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.
Add a second Application Load Balancer in the same Region for redundancy.

explanation: To achieve 99.99% availability (approximately 52 minutes of downtime per year), a multi-Region architecture is essential. A single Region, regardless of how many AZs are used, cannot guarantee 99.99% availability due to the possibility of Region-wide events. Deploying in a second Region with Aurora Global Database for data replication and Route 53 failover routing enables automatic traffic redirection if the primary Region becomes unavailable. Option B adds resilience within the Region but doesn't protect against Region-level failures. Option C improves single-Region resilience but still has a single Region of failure. Option D adds no meaningful redundancy as ALB is already highly available.

stem: A media company needs to process uploaded video files by extracting thumbnails, transcoding to multiple resolutions, and generating subtitles. Each step depends on the completion of the previous step. Some steps may fail and need to be retried. The workflow must handle thousands of concurrent video processing jobs. Which AWS service should orchestrate this workflow?

options.text: AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow with state management, error handling, and retry logic.
Amazon SQS with separate queues for each processing step.
AWS Lambda with direct invocations chained together for each processing step.
Amazon EventBridge rules triggered by each step's completion event.

explanation: AWS Step Functions is designed for orchestrating multi-step workflows with built-in state management, error handling, retry logic, and parallel execution. It provides visual workflow monitoring and can coordinate AWS services like Lambda, ECS, and MediaConvert. Step Functions Express Workflows can handle thousands of concurrent executions. The sequential dependency between steps maps perfectly to Step Functions' state machine model. Option B requires custom orchestration logic and doesn't provide built-in retry or state management. Option C creates tight coupling and doesn't handle failures gracefully. Option D works for event-driven architectures but lacks the sequential workflow orchestration and retry capabilities of Step Functions.

stem: A company uses Amazon RDS MySQL with a db.r5.2xlarge instance for its production database. The database has 1 TB of data, and AWS Compute Optimizer shows that the CPU utilization averages 15% with peaks at 35%. Memory utilization is at 40%. The company wants to reduce database costs. What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Migrate to Amazon Aurora MySQL, which offers better price-performance and can handle the same workload with a smaller instance.
Right-size the instance to db.r5.xlarge, which provides sufficient capacity for the current utilization levels.
Switch to a db.t3.2xlarge instance for lower cost with burstable performance.
Move the database to Amazon DynamoDB for lower costs per transaction.

explanation: With CPU averaging 15% and peaking at 35%, and memory at 40%, the db.r5.2xlarge is significantly over-provisioned. Right-sizing to db.r5.xlarge (half the CPU and memory) would still provide ample headroom with peak CPU at approximately 70% and memory at 80%. This reduces the instance cost by approximately 50% while maintaining the same engine and requiring no application changes. Option A could offer better performance but involves migration effort and potential compatibility considerations. Option C burstable instances are generally not recommended for production databases with sustained workloads. Option D requires a complete application rewrite to change from relational to NoSQL.

stem: A company needs to implement encryption for data at rest and in transit for an application running on Amazon EC2 that uses Amazon RDS PostgreSQL. Which TWO actions should a solutions architect take? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Enable SSL/TLS on the RDS PostgreSQL instance and configure the application to use SSL connections with the rds-ca certificate bundle.
Enable RDS storage encryption using an AWS KMS key when creating the database instance.
Use a self-signed SSL certificate on the EC2 instance for encrypting application traffic.
Store the database password in plaintext in the application configuration file and restrict file permissions.
Enable Amazon S3 server-side encryption for the RDS backup files.

explanation: Enabling SSL/TLS connections between the application and RDS encrypts data in transit, protecting it from eavesdropping. AWS provides certificate bundles for RDS that the application can use to verify the database server's identity. Enabling RDS storage encryption with KMS encrypts data at rest, including the database files, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots. Together, these two measures provide comprehensive encryption at rest and in transit. Option C doesn't address database encryption. Option D is a security anti-pattern. Option E is unnecessary because RDS backups inherit the encryption setting from the database instance.

stem: A company needs to deploy a new version of its application with zero downtime. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group. The company wants the ability to quickly roll back to the previous version if issues are detected. Which deployment strategy should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Perform a rolling deployment by updating instances one at a time in the existing Auto Scaling group.
Create a new Auto Scaling group with the new version, register it with the ALB, shift traffic gradually using weighted target groups, and deregister the old group if successful.
Stop all running instances simultaneously, deploy the new version, and start the instances.
Use Amazon S3 to host the new application version and update the EC2 instances to download it at startup.

explanation: A blue/green deployment using a new Auto Scaling group with weighted target groups provides zero downtime and easy rollback. The new group (green) is fully tested alongside the old group (blue). Traffic is gradually shifted using target group weights. If issues are detected, traffic is immediately shifted back to the blue group by adjusting weights. Once validated, the blue group is deregistered and terminated. Option A has partial downtime risk during updates and slower rollback. Option C causes complete downtime. Option D doesn't address deployment strategy or rollback capability.

stem: A financial trading company needs a database solution that provides single-digit millisecond latency for read and write operations at any scale. The database must support ACID transactions and store structured data with complex queries. The data model involves many-to-many relationships between entities. Which database service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB for single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.
Amazon Aurora with reader endpoints for distributing read traffic.
Amazon Neptune for managing complex relationships between entities.
Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra) for wide-column data storage.

explanation: Amazon Aurora provides single-digit millisecond read latency, supports ACID transactions, and excels at complex SQL queries including joins for many-to-many relationships. Aurora can scale reads using up to 15 read replicas with a reader endpoint for load balancing. It combines the performance of commercial databases with the simplicity of open-source databases. Option A provides low latency but doesn't natively support complex relational queries or many-to-many relationships without denormalization. Option C is optimized for graph traversals, not traditional relational queries. Option D is a wide-column store that doesn't support complex joins or ACID transactions across partitions.

stem: A company uses Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and has set up detailed monitoring for 100 EC2 instances, 50 custom metrics with 1-minute granularity, and 20 CloudWatch dashboards. The monthly CloudWatch bill has become significant. Which actions can reduce CloudWatch costs without losing critical monitoring capabilities?

options.text: Switch from detailed monitoring (1-minute) to basic monitoring (5-minute) for non-critical instances and consolidate dashboards.
Disable all CloudWatch monitoring and rely on application logs for troubleshooting.
Move all custom metrics to Amazon S3 and query them with Athena when needed.
Replace CloudWatch with a self-managed Prometheus and Grafana setup on EC2 instances.

explanation: Switching from detailed monitoring (1-minute intervals, paid) to basic monitoring (5-minute intervals, free) for non-critical instances eliminates per-instance monitoring charges. Consolidating dashboards reduces dashboard costs (first 3 are free, $3/month each after that). These changes maintain monitoring capabilities for critical resources while reducing costs for less important ones. Option B eliminates monitoring entirely, which is risky. Option C loses real-time monitoring capabilities. Option D introduces significant operational overhead for managing monitoring infrastructure.

stem: A company is implementing a Zero Trust architecture for its AWS workloads. The company wants to verify the identity and security posture of every device before allowing access to internal applications running on EC2 instances. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to implement this?

options.text: AWS Verified Access to provide secure access to corporate applications without requiring a VPN.
AWS Client VPN with multi-factor authentication for all users.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN with strict security group rules.
Amazon CloudFront with signed URLs for application access.

explanation: AWS Verified Access implements Zero Trust principles by evaluating each access request against defined policies that consider user identity, device security posture, and other contextual signals before granting access to applications. It eliminates the need for a VPN and provides fine-grained access control. Verified Access integrates with identity providers and device management solutions. Option B uses a VPN which is network-centric, not Zero Trust (grants network access rather than application-level access). Option C is for site-to-site connectivity, not individual device verification. Option D provides content delivery security, not device posture verification.

stem: A company runs a critical application that writes data to Amazon EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances. The company needs to protect against data loss from accidental deletion or corruption of EBS volumes. The recovery point objective is 1 hour. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) policies to automatically take EBS snapshots every hour.
Write a cron job on each EC2 instance to create EBS snapshots every hour using the AWS CLI.
Use AWS Backup to create a backup plan that takes hourly EBS snapshots with defined retention policies.
Replicate data from EBS to Amazon S3 every hour using a custom script.

explanation: AWS Backup provides a centralized, fully managed backup service with support for EBS volumes. Backup plans can be configured to take hourly snapshots with defined retention and lifecycle policies. AWS Backup also supports cross-Region and cross-account backup for additional protection. This provides the least operational overhead compared to custom solutions. Option A also works well but AWS Backup provides more comprehensive features like cross-account backup and centralized management. Option B requires managing scripts on every instance. Option D requires custom scripting and doesn't leverage EBS snapshot capabilities.

stem: A company is building a search feature for its e-commerce website. The search must support full-text search, faceted navigation, auto-complete suggestions, and handle typos in search queries. The product catalog has 5 million items. Which AWS service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service (successor to Amazon Elasticsearch Service) for full-text search with fuzzy matching and aggregation support.
Amazon DynamoDB with a Global Secondary Index on the product name attribute.
Amazon RDS with FULLTEXT indexes for search functionality.
Amazon CloudSearch for managed search with auto-scaling.

explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Service provides full-text search with features like fuzzy matching (handling typos), auto-complete (using completion suggesters), faceted search (using aggregations), and relevance scoring. It's designed for search-intensive workloads and can handle millions of documents with sub-second query latency. Option B doesn't support full-text search, fuzzy matching, or faceted navigation. Option C provides basic full-text search but lacks the advanced features like fuzzy matching, auto-complete, and efficient faceted search at scale. Option D is being deprecated in favor of OpenSearch Service and has fewer features.

stem: A company is building a multi-account AWS environment and wants to centralize security findings from Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie across all accounts. Which approach provides centralized visibility?

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub with organization integration in the management account to aggregate findings from all member accounts and all security services.
Configure each service to send findings to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket using event notifications.
Create a custom Lambda function that queries each service's API in each account and stores results in DynamoDB.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to aggregate security findings from all accounts into a central log group.

explanation: AWS Security Hub provides a centralized dashboard that aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes security findings from multiple AWS services (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and more) and third-party tools. With AWS Organizations integration, Security Hub can be enabled as a delegated administrator to automatically aggregate findings from all member accounts. This provides a single pane of glass for security across the organization. Option B requires custom integration for each service. Option C is operationally complex and fragile. Option D doesn't provide a security-focused dashboard or correlation capabilities.

stem: A company has a data lake in Amazon S3 with 500 TB of data. Data scientists run ad-hoc queries using Amazon Athena, and the monthly Athena costs are high because queries scan large amounts of data. Which TWO optimization strategies should a solutions architect implement to reduce Athena query costs?

options.text: Convert data from CSV/JSON to Apache Parquet or ORC columnar formats and partition the data by commonly filtered columns.
Move the data from S3 to Amazon EBS volumes for faster access.
Increase the number of Athena workgroups to distribute the query load.
Use Athena workgroups with per-query data scan limits to control costs and require data scientists to use SELECT with specific columns instead of SELECT *.

explanation: Converting data to columnar formats (Parquet/ORC) dramatically reduces the data scanned because Athena reads only the columns needed for the query instead of entire rows. Partitioning by commonly filtered columns (e.g., date, region) allows Athena to skip irrelevant data partitions entirely. Together, these optimizations can reduce data scanned (and therefore costs) by 90% or more. Additionally, workgroup scan limits and avoiding SELECT * further control costs. Option B moves data off S3 which is incompatible with Athena. Option C doesn't reduce the amount of data scanned per query.

stem: A company runs a microservices application on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. Some services occasionally fail due to transient errors when calling downstream services. The company wants to implement a pattern that prevents cascading failures when a downstream service is unhealthy. Which pattern should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Implement the circuit breaker pattern using AWS App Mesh to detect failing downstream services and stop sending requests to them until they recover.
Increase the timeout values for all downstream service calls to allow more time for responses.
Add more Fargate tasks for each service to handle increased load during failures.
Implement synchronous retry logic with unlimited retries for all downstream calls.

explanation: The circuit breaker pattern prevents cascading failures by detecting when a downstream service is unhealthy and temporarily stopping requests to it. AWS App Mesh provides built-in circuit breaker functionality as part of its service mesh capabilities for ECS services. When the circuit breaker opens, requests immediately fail fast instead of waiting for timeouts, protecting the calling service and giving the downstream service time to recover. Option B increases timeouts which can make cascading failures worse by tying up resources. Option C adds capacity but doesn't address the root cause of cascading failures. Option D with unlimited retries would overwhelm the failing downstream service.

stem: A company is building a serverless data processing pipeline. Files are uploaded to Amazon S3, which triggers an AWS Lambda function for processing. Some files are very large (up to 5 GB) and processing them takes more than 15 minutes. Lambda has a maximum execution time of 15 minutes. Which alternative architecture should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use S3 event notifications to trigger an AWS Step Functions workflow that launches an AWS Fargate task to process the large files.
Split the Lambda function into multiple functions that process the file in parallel, each within the 15-minute limit.
Increase the Lambda memory to 10 GB to speed up processing and complete within 15 minutes.
Use Lambda layers to extend the maximum execution time beyond 15 minutes.

explanation: AWS Fargate tasks do not have the 15-minute time limit of Lambda functions and can run for as long as needed. Using S3 event notifications to trigger a Step Functions workflow that orchestrates a Fargate task provides a serverless solution for long-running file processing. Step Functions manages the workflow, error handling, and retries. Option B may work for parallelizable tasks but adds significant complexity and not all file processing can be parallelized. Option C may speed up some workloads but cannot guarantee completion within 15 minutes for 5 GB files. Option D is incorrect because Lambda layers cannot extend the execution time limit.

stem: A company wants to ensure that all IAM users in their AWS account have multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled. Any user without MFA should be denied access to all AWS services except the ability to set up their own MFA device. Which IAM policy strategy implements this requirement?

options.text: Create an IAM policy that denies all actions except IAM self-service MFA actions when MFA is not present in the request context, and attach it to all IAM users.
Enable MFA on the AWS account root user only, as it automatically enforces MFA for all IAM users.
Use an SCP in AWS Organizations to require MFA for all API calls.
Configure AWS Config to detect users without MFA and automatically delete their access keys.

explanation: An IAM policy with a condition checking aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent can deny all actions except IAM MFA self-service actions (iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice, iam:EnableMFADevice, etc.) when MFA is not present. This forces users to set up MFA before they can do anything else. The policy uses a Deny with a condition of aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent being false, with an exception for MFA management actions. Option B doesn't enforce MFA for IAM users. Option C requires Organizations and applies to the account level, not individual users. Option D is reactive rather than preventive and deleting access keys is destructive.

stem: A company runs a production Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with 1 writer instance and 3 reader instances, all db.r6g.2xlarge. Read traffic has decreased by 50% after implementing caching. The company wants to reduce database costs while maintaining the ability to handle read traffic spikes. Which approach should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Remove 2 reader instances and keep 1 reader for read traffic.
Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for read replicas with a minimum of 1 and maximum of 3 replicas based on CPU utilization.
Switch all instances to db.r6g.xlarge for cost savings.
Migrate to Aurora Serverless v2 for the reader instances while keeping the writer as provisioned.

explanation: Aurora Auto Scaling for read replicas automatically adjusts the number of reader instances based on demand. With a minimum of 1 replica for normal traffic (after caching reduced reads by 50%) and a maximum of 3 for spike handling, the company maintains resilience while reducing costs during normal operations. This saves on 2 reader instances during most of the time while automatically scaling up when needed. Option A permanently removes capacity with no ability to handle spikes. Option C reduces per-instance cost but still over-provisions readers. Option D works but may be more expensive than Auto Scaling between 1-3 provisioned replicas for predictable traffic patterns.

stem: A company is migrating an on-premises application to AWS. The application requires a shared file system that can be accessed by multiple EC2 instances simultaneously across different Availability Zones. The application uses a Linux-based operating system and requires POSIX-compliant file access. Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) Multi-Attach volumes shared across instances.
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) with mount targets in each Availability Zone.
Amazon S3 with S3 File Gateway for file-based access.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for shared file access.

explanation: Amazon EFS provides a fully managed, elastic, POSIX-compliant shared file system that can be concurrently accessed by thousands of EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. Mount targets in each AZ enable low-latency access from instances in that AZ. EFS automatically scales capacity as files are added or removed. Option A EBS Multi-Attach is limited to io1/io2 volumes within a single AZ and requires a cluster-aware file system. Option C provides file access through a gateway but adds latency and doesn't provide true POSIX compliance. Option D is designed for Windows workloads using SMB protocol, not Linux/POSIX.

stem: A gaming company needs to maintain a global leaderboard that is updated in real time as players complete games. The leaderboard must support millions of concurrent reads and thousands of writes per second. Players need to query their rank and see the top 100 players with sub-millisecond latency. Which database solution is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis using sorted sets for the leaderboard.
Amazon DynamoDB with a Global Secondary Index on the score attribute.
Amazon RDS MySQL with an index on the score column and ORDER BY queries.
Amazon Aurora with read replicas for distributing leaderboard read queries.

explanation: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with sorted sets is the ideal solution for real-time leaderboards. Redis sorted sets provide O(log(N)) time complexity for adding scores and O(log(N)+M) for range queries (top N). ZRANGEBYSCORE, ZRANK, and ZREVRANGE commands directly support leaderboard operations with sub-millisecond latency. Redis handles millions of operations per second. Option B DynamoDB doesn't efficiently support ranking across all items. Option C cannot handle millions of concurrent reads with sub-millisecond latency. Option D still has single-digit millisecond latency and ranking queries on millions of rows are expensive.

stem: A company has deployed AWS Lambda functions that access Amazon RDS databases in a private subnet. The Lambda functions are configured with VPC access. The security team notices that the Lambda functions are using a NAT gateway to access other AWS services like Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB, increasing costs. How can the solutions architect reduce NAT gateway usage while maintaining security?

options.text: Remove VPC configuration from the Lambda functions and access RDS through a public endpoint.
Create VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB so Lambda can access these services without going through the NAT gateway.
Move the Lambda functions to a public subnet with an internet gateway.
Increase the NAT gateway capacity to reduce per-GB data processing charges.

explanation: VPC gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route traffic directly through the AWS network without using the NAT gateway, eliminating NAT gateway data processing charges for these services. Gateway endpoints are free and provide secure, private connectivity. The Lambda functions remain in the VPC for RDS access while accessing S3 and DynamoDB through the endpoints.
